summary: Describes how to provide authentication and confidentiality to OSPFv3 by using the IPv6 Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload extension headers. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Routers tell each other where roads lead. This explains how to put a lock and a signature on those messages so a fake router cannot trick the real ones.

questions: how to secure ospfv3 with ipsec
does ospfv3 support ah and esp
why does ospfv3 use manual keys
subtitle: How OSPFv3 routers use IPsec AH and ESP headers to authenticate, and optionally encrypt, their routing messages.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3, OSPF for IPv6, dropped the authentication fields that OSPFv2 had in its header, so something else must protect routing messages from forgery.
tldr.mechanism: OSPFv3 packets are protected with the IPv6 Authentication Header or Encapsulating Security Payload, using transport mode and manually configured keys with the same SA parameters in both directions.
tldr.outcome: Authentication is required and confidentiality is recommended. Because the keys are manual, the design offers no replay protection, which the RFC says leaves OSPF open to replay attacks.

today: RFC 4552 is a Proposed Standard from June 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OSPF version 2 puts AuType and Authentication fields in its protocol header. In OSPFv3, the version of OSPF for IPv6, both fields were removed. OSPFv3 instead relies on the IPv6 Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) to provide integrity, authentication and confidentiality.

RFC 4552 describes how those extension headers are used for OSPFv3. It assumes the reader already knows OSPFv3, AH, ESP, security associations, tunnel and transport mode, and the key management options for AH and ESP (manual keying and IKE).
sections.eli5: The old routing message had a little box for a password. The new one removed the box, so this RFC says to wrap the whole message in an official security envelope instead.

sections.title: Modes, Authentication and Confidentiality
sections.content:
A transport mode security association is generally used between two hosts. It must be a tunnel mode SA if either end is a router or gateway. OSPFv3 packets travel between routers but are delivered locally, so the routers act as hosts. Implementations MUST support transport mode SAs and MAY also support tunnel mode.

Implementations MUST support authentication. They MUST support ESP and MAY support AH. ESP in transport mode authenticates only the OSPFv3 packet, not the IPv6 header, extension headers or options. AH in transport mode also covers selected portions of the IPv6 header, extension headers and options. When authentication is on, packets not protected with AH or ESP, and packets that fail the checks, MUST be silently discarded.

Implementations SHOULD support confidentiality, and if it is provided, ESP MUST be used. Packets not protected with ESP, or failing the checks, MUST be silently discarded.
sections.eli5: Every routing message must carry a signature or be sealed in a locked envelope. Anything without the right seal is thrown away without a word.

sections.title: What IPsec Must Provide
sections.content:
OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 share IP protocol number 89 and are told apart by the OSPF header version number. IPsec selectors cannot use arbitrary protocol-specific header fields, so the OSPF version field is not usable. Because OSPFv2 is only for IPv4 and OSPFv3 only for IPv6, the IP version field tells them apart.

The implementation MUST support transport mode, multiple SPDs with a selection function based on interface, source address, destination address, protocol and direction as selectors, tagging of inbound packets with the interface ID, and manually configured keys. It MUST NOT let the user choose stream ciphers, since they are not suitable for manual keys. The routing module SHOULD be able to configure, modify and delete IPsec rules on the fly, mainly to secure virtual links.

IP encapsulation of ESP MUST be supported, while UDP encapsulation SHOULD NOT be used. Multiple SAs with the same selectors between a sender and receiver MUST be supported, so different DSCP classes can use different SAs.
sections.eli5: For this to work, the security system has to be able to tell which door a message came in through, accept hand-set keys, and be changed while running.

sections.title: Why Manual Keys
sections.content:
OSPFv3 uses multicast and unicast packets. On a broadcast interface the protection must be one to many. IKE is based on Diffie-Hellman and works only between two parties, so it cannot provide this. The specification therefore mandates manual keying, where SAs are statically installed on the routers. Future work could explore protocols such as KINK or GSAKMP.

The RFC argues that using different SAs for inbound and outbound traffic cannot work well. If A and B use SAa and SAb, a new router C has no SA that both A and B can understand. Giving every node its own outbound SA and installing all of them everywhere works, but does not scale and every new node means a new SA on every other node. So implementations MUST use manually configured keys with the same SA parameters (SPI, keys and so on) for inbound and outbound SAs.

Keys MUST be configurable in hexadecimal rather than a restricted ASCII subset, because a restricted character set reduces key entropy significantly.
sections.eli5: When a whole classroom talks at once, a separate secret code for every pair of kids would be a mess. So everyone uses one shared code, set up by hand ahead of time.

sections.title: SA Granularity and Virtual Links
sections.content:
The user SHOULD be able to share one SA among several interfaces or use a unique SA per interface. OSPFv3 can run multiple instances on one interface using the Instance Id field, but IPsec cannot select on that field, so all instances on an interface use the same SA. In OSPFv3 terms, SAs are per-link and not per-interface.

Virtual links MUST have a different SA from the underlying interface. Packets on virtual links use unicast non-link-local IPv6 source addresses, which sets them apart. The endpoint addresses are learned only during routing table computation, so the routing module must install the SPD and SAD entries before the exchange starts. Manual SA parameters are preconfigured but installed only once the addresses are known.

To make addresses predictable, routers MUST pick the first IPv6 address with the LA-bit set in the transit area's intra-area-prefix LSAs as the source address. They MUST pick the first such address received from the virtual neighbor as the destination. Multiple LSAs are treated as concatenated and ordered by ascending Link State ID.
sections.eli5: A tunnel between two far-apart routers needs its own lock, and both ends need to agree ahead of time on which address to use, so the lock knows which messages to expect.

sections.title: Changing Keys Without Dropping Adjacencies
sections.content:
Keys SHOULD be changed periodically. A three-step rekeying procedure SHOULD be provided so a link can be rekeyed without dropping OSPFv3 packets or disrupting the adjacency. On every router on the link: create an additional inbound SA with a new SPI and key; replace the outbound SA with one using the new SPI and key, atomically with respect to sending; then remove the original inbound SA.

All routers must finish a step before any begins the next. One way to pace this is a configurable KeyRolloverInterval: a router waits that interval after starting step 1, and again after step 2. All routers on a link should use the same value, long enough for the administrator to change keys everywhere, and the administrator chooses it.

The RFC recommends that keys SHOULD be changed at least every 90 days. It reasons that the weakest combination is NULL encryption (ESP) or no encryption (AH) with HMAC-MD5 authentication, and that RFC 3562's analysis for the TCP MD5 option also applies here.
sections.eli5: To swap locks without anyone getting shut out, first everybody learns to open the new lock, then everybody starts using it, and only then is the old lock thrown away.

sections.title: The Protection Barrier and SPD Rules
sections.content:
The IPsec protection barrier MUST be around the OSPF protocol, so all inbound and outbound OSPF traffic goes through IPsec processing. For interfaces with OSPFv3 security disabled, the SPD has a single rule: OSPF is bypassed. For interfaces with it enabled, there are rules for traffic from fe80::/10 (link-local) and, for virtual links, rules for specific source and destination /128 addresses.

The virtual link rules MUST be installed on the interfaces connected to the transit area, and MAY be installed on all interfaces. Without them everywhere, clear text or malicious packets with the virtual link endpoint addresses could reach OSPFv3. OSPFv3 would still drop them as they came in on the wrong interface. Installing them everywhere adds processing on interfaces with no other IPsec work, and the RFC calls this an implementation choice that does not affect interoperability.
sections.eli5: A guard stands at the door of every routing room. Rooms with security on only let in properly sealed messages. Rooms with it off wave everything through.

sections.title: Replay and Other Limits
sections.content:
It is not possible with current standards to provide complete replay protection with manual keying, so this solution does not protect against replay attacks. Sequence numbers cannot be negotiated. The RFC says replaying OSPF packets can disrupt adjacencies, lead to a denial of service, cause the database exchange process to run continuously with CPU overload, and cause micro loops.

The design protects against the vulnerabilities identified for cryptographic authentication in the cited OSPF analysis, with exceptions. Manual keys are usually long lived, giving an attacker time to discover them, and an administrator may configure weak keys (there are known weak keys for DES and 3DES). Using the same key on all routers on a link means that one compromised, malfunctioning or misconfigured router can impersonate others.
sections.eli5: The stamp proves who wrote a message, but not when. A sneaky router could replay an old, genuine message and confuse everyone. Using one shared key also means one bad router can pretend to be any of them.

THE THREE REKEYING STEPS ON EVERY ROUTER (RFC 4552)

items.title: Step 1
items.text: Add an extra inbound SA with the new SPI and key.

items.title: Step 2
items.text: Replace the outbound SA with the new SPI and key, atomically.
